scenes.title: The blank document
scenes.narration: The document is open. At the top it says, Q3 Innovation Plan. The cursor blinks. Your inbox is full of requests, your team wants a direction, and somebody wants a polished plan by Friday. I know that room. The pressure makes the blank page feel like the problem. So you open a tool, ask for ideas, and in thirty seconds you have a confident looking answer. Now what? Who will decide which idea matters? What evidence would make that choice responsible? What data did you put into the tool to get there? A beautiful page can hide those questions for a little while. It cannot answer them. In the opening of Accelerated, I start with that blinking cursor because it is familiar. The book begins with product teams carrying noise, conflicting priorities, and documents that do not move decisions. The work here is to give the team a way to learn, choose, and keep its judgment when the page fills up.

scenes.title: What a product system does
scenes.narration: A product system sounds larger than it needs to be. Think about the last idea that arrived in a meeting. Someone noticed a customer problem. Someone else had a competing story. A third person asked for a number nobody had. The team left with another document to write. A system gives those moments a path. It helps you record the signal, name the decision, state what you believe, and come back to what happened. AI can help organize messy input, test the shape of an argument, and make a first draft. The judgment still belongs to people who understand the consequences. That is the argument in the first chapter. I describe AI as a strategy partner, a signal amplifier, and a structure builder. Those are jobs it may help with, under the right conditions. They are not permission to trust every output. If it gives you five polished options, you still need to ask who benefits, what is missing, and which option you can test safely. Speed can create room to think. It can also fill that room with more noise.

scenes.title: The map, with the book underneath
scenes.narration: Look at this map. Signals. Alignment. Momentum. It is a way to navigate the workshop. First, take the raw material coming at you and find a question worth answering. Then give the people carrying the decision a shared direction. Then build a rhythm that lets the next round of evidence change the plan. The book organizes its printed chapters as Systems, Align, and Momentum. The workshop uses the three labels on this existing infographic as a visual guide. You will see where those paths cross; the graphic is not a replacement for the chapters. In these first lessons we stay close to the signal side. We will choose one decision, work backward to evidence, and ask what a small test could teach us. There is a human thread through the book, too: Sam, a product manager who has talent but keeps getting pulled into reactive work. That story makes the pressure visible. It is a teaching story from the book, not a claim about a current customer. Keep that distinction in view as we move between story, worksheet, and public proof.

scenes.title: Safety before tools
scenes.narration: Before you try any prompt, decide what information can leave your desk. The book's data-safety note comes before the chapters for a reason. Customer details, finances, internal strategy, and company records can carry obligations that a convenient text box does not erase. My working rule for this course is simple: use public information, material your organization has approved for that use, or a made-up example. If you are unsure, stop and check the policy that governs your work. Do not put restricted material into an external model to make the worksheet feel realistic. We can learn the method with a synthetic case. Imagine a team trying to improve the first week for new members. We can invent a harmless request list and test our reasoning without using anyone's account, message, or history. On the screen, watch the example move into a three-column boundary: public, approved internal, restricted. “Approved internal” means approved for this particular tool and purpose, not merely available to you at work. This boundary follows the decision file through every lesson. It is part of product judgment, not an appendix.

scenes.title: Make the cover sheet
scenes.narration: Let's make the first page of your decision file. It starts with a decision, not a tool. Write one sentence: “We need to decide whether to...” It could be whether to change an onboarding step, simplify a service request, or test a different way to explain an offer. Keep the scope small enough that someone could make a choice after seeing evidence. Now write who owns that choice and when it must be made. If nobody owns it, name the role you need to ask. Underneath, write what would go wrong if you guessed. Then mark the inputs you might want to use. Public, approved for this purpose, or restricted. If the real inputs are restricted, make a safe stand-in. Preserve the shape of the problem; remove the person and the private facts. You are allowed to pause the video while you write. When you resume, you should have a cover sheet a colleague could read without asking what you are trying to decide. You should also know which inputs will stay out of any AI tool. That is a useful first result, even if the plan itself is still unfinished.

scenes.title: Human ownership
scenes.narration: Take one more look at your sentence. Could a fast draft make that decision for you? Probably not. It might help you list options, put questions in order, or notice that an assumption is doing too much work. But a person still has to decide what matters and what risk the team is willing to carry. That is why I ask you to keep the decision file. A chat window can be useful for a moment; the file makes the reasoning visible when the moment has passed. Write one line under the cover: “What would I need to learn before I choose?” Do not answer it yet. Let the question sit. In the next lesson we will bring that question into a crowded planning room. We will look at three possible paths and choose one worth testing. If you have only a vague problem now, that is enough. A good first page does not pretend to know the answer. It tells the truth about the decision, the evidence you have, and the information you have permission to use. Keep that first page open. The rest of this workshop will build on it.

scenes.title: Fifteen priorities
scenes.narration: The meeting has barely started and the board is full. Fifteen roadmap items. Fifteen top priorities. The person asking for retention has a good reason. So does the person asking for revenue. The refactor matters to the engineers who will carry the system next quarter. Everybody can defend their note. That is why the room is stuck. In Chapter Two, I tell a version of this planning meeting and ask what the team cannot afford to get wrong. That question changes the shape of the conversation. The book's case lands on the first minutes of a new user's experience. We do not need to borrow that answer for every team. We need to borrow the move: step away from the list and name the consequence of a wrong choice. Open the decision file from Lesson One. Read the decision at the top. If it still sounds like “choose all the good ideas,” make it sharper. Whose experience or business result is at stake? What would a choice teach you before the next planning cycle?

scenes.title: What the list hides
scenes.narration: A long list can feel fair. Each person sees their concern represented. But the list does not tell you which problem to solve first, and it cannot tell you why. That is the trap in the chapter. More information may give every proposal a stronger defense while leaving the actual decision untouched. Think about airport signage. A terminal can offer plenty of services, yet the traveler needs to know where to go next. If the sign does not make that clear, more decoration will not help. The same thing happens in a product meeting. Before asking an AI tool for twenty feature ideas, ask what path the person is trying to find and what the team can change. Here is a synthetic case we will use on screen: a small membership service has three requests. Rewrite its welcome email. Add a guided first task. Build a dashboard for staff. They might all help. We do not know yet. Our job is to compare them against the same decision, rather than letting the loudest request become the plan.

scenes.title: Match the frame to the question
scenes.narration: Chapter Three gives us a way to structure a messy opportunity. The first move is to decide what question the case is answering. If you are asking whether a market is attractive, the book offers a market frame. If you are choosing a product or segment, it offers three C plus P: customer, company, competition, product. We are choosing a product move, so that second frame fits. Customer: which request responds to a real, urgent job? Company: what can this team actually deliver and maintain? Competition: how is the need handled now, even if the alternative is a spreadsheet or another person? Product: what is the smallest offer that could show value? scenes.title: Compare without fake precision
scenes.narration: Now put the three options side by side. For each one, write the customer pain it might address, the business reason to care, the learning value of trying it, the risk, and whether you can reverse the choice. scenes.title: Economic fit belongs in the case
scenes.narration: There is another question that can make a promising idea fail: how does the value reach a customer, and how does the work sustain itself? Chapter Three brings business model options into the case after the customer and product question is clear. It asks whether people need to experience value before paying, whether value accumulates over time, whether a free tier is affordable, and whether usage is predictable. An AI brainstorm can offer possibilities. It cannot supply the missing customer and operating evidence by sounding certain.

scenes.title: Make a reversible choice
scenes.narration: For the sample case, I would choose a small test of the guided first task. I would not commit to a full guided onboarding product. I would show a simple first step to a few consenting participants through an approved research process, then ask whether it helped them begin. I would keep the welcome email as an alternative if the test shows the language is confusing. I would hold the staff dashboard until the team knows which question it needs the dashboard to answer. My reason is not that guided tasks always win. It is that this option can test the starting-point assumption while keeping the next commitment small. Your decision may go another way. Put your choice at the top of the page and write the sentence that makes it defensible: “We choose this because...” Then record the two alternatives you are setting aside. Give each one a real reason, not a vague “lower priority.” A decision file that only celebrates the winner loses half the learning. When new evidence arrives, those alternatives tell you what you thought you were trading away.

scenes.title: A dashboard in the room
scenes.narration: Imagine walking into a review with a dashboard redesign. You have evidence that people struggle with the current screen. You have a proposed fix. You put up the first slide and someone asks, “Is this the best use of engineering time right now?” That is a reasonable question. It may feel like a rejection, but it is also a clue. scenes.title: Work backward from the choice
scenes.narration: Open the priority page you made in Lesson Two. You chose one path and wrote an assumption that could overturn it. Now write the decision owner’s question in their words. It tells you what evidence the decision needs. The chapter argues that insight can land flat when its frame ignores the risk the other person carries. scenes.title: Keep alternatives visible
scenes.narration: A single polished idea invites a yes or no. Chapter Four calls this the binary trap. The dashboard case becomes easier to discuss when the team can compare a quick simplification, a deeper rebuild, and a deliberate delay. Each path has a different cost and a different thing it could teach. Your priority file already has two alternatives. Bring them forward rather than hiding them after you choose. For the membership example, the welcome email could be the light change. The guided task is the small behavior test. The staff dashboard is a visibility investment. None of those labels is a fact about customers. They are ways to make the trade visible. If the objection is “We are solving the wrong part of onboarding,” the evidence should tell you where a person stops and why. If the objection is “We cannot support another workflow,” the evidence may need to include staff effort. A stronger frame does not mean louder language. It means the choice is clear enough for another person to challenge.

scenes.title: Ask what would change your mind
scenes.narration: Suppose you can ask only one more question before the review. What would change your mind? That question keeps discovery honest. If you would make the same recommendation no matter what the answer is, you may be collecting support for a story rather than testing it. An AI tool can help you rehearse the questions. It cannot turn a simulated objection into a customer interview. On our card, write one evidence gap that matters. Maybe we do not know whether people abandon the first step because they cannot find it, cannot understand it, or do not value it. Those are different problems. scenes.title: Design a small evidence move
scenes.narration: Let's fill the rest of the card. The decision is whether to test a guided first task. Our current answer is yes, because the team suspects people need a clearer starting point. The strongest objection is that the first step may already be clear; maybe the real issue comes later. The missing evidence is an observation of where people hesitate and a short question about what they expected to happen next. A safe test could use a prototype and willing participants under an approved research process. We would record what they did, what they said, and what remains uncertain. That last field matters. A few observations can direct the next question; they do not establish a population-wide result. If you have no approved research access, keep the card as a plan. Do not manufacture quotes or silently substitute simulated people for participants. The dashboard case in the book helps us see how a named trade can make evidence relevant. Our exercise turns that lesson into an action you can take without pretending that the answer is already known.

scenes.title: Carry the question forward
scenes.narration: Pause and make your own card. Write the decision in a sentence. Write the answer you currently believe. Write the strongest fair objection. Then write one piece of evidence that could change the decision and a safe way to seek it. If your evidence is already available, record its source and date. If it is missing, say missing. Your file should now show a line from priority choice to evidence gap. That line is the point of these first three lessons. A good question can save you from a month of defending the wrong artifact. When you resume, look at the person behind the evidence. We tend to summarize that person as a persona and leave the slide untouched for a year. In the next lesson we will make the customer situation more specific and the persona easier to revise. You do not have to win the room with a perfect story today. You need a decision that another person can understand, an objection you have taken seriously, and evidence you would actually listen to. Keep the card attached to your priority page. We are going to use it again.

scenes.title: The large idea returns
scenes.narration: We are back at the Q3 Innovation Plan. The page is no longer empty. You have chosen a priority and written down the evidence that could change your mind. But the broad idea is still sitting there: improve the member experience. Maybe your version says transform onboarding, reinvent support, or use AI to personalize everything. Those ambitions can be useful. They are hard to test as a single bet. Chapter Five of Accelerated opens with an empty planning document and asks us to think big while building small. The first move is to shrink the question. Instead of “What should we build for everyone?” ask, “What is one moment we can understand better this week?” In our fictional membership service, that moment is the first task after someone joins. A small prototype can show us whether the instruction helps a person begin. It cannot prove the whole program works. That is fine. The point of a small test is to let reality correct the plan before the plan becomes expensive.

scenes.title: The persona deck
scenes.narration: Now picture the persona deck beside that plan. It looks finished. There is a stock photo, a name, a city, a favorite app, and a line about wanting convenience. In Chapter Six, I describe a gorgeous deck that did not help my team make decisions. That is an uncomfortable confession because the work looked careful. The question was whether the details pointed to a real moment in the product. If we say our member is thirty-four and busy, what should the team do differently on the first task? We do not know. If we say the member needs to understand where to start without asking for help, we can observe a situation, compare a design, and notice what we missed. The first statement paints a person. The second names a job in context. Do not throw away demographic information when it is genuinely relevant and responsibly gathered. Just do not let a polished portrait stand in for evidence about behavior. The persona has to earn its place in the decision.

scenes.title: From who to what
scenes.narration: The book makes this shift with Sarah. A static description tells us who she supposedly is. A job description asks what she is trying to do in a particular moment. In the book example, she is preparing for a Monday meeting and needs progress updates without sending messages that make her feel like a micromanager. That gives a team something to work with. There is a time pressure, a current workaround, and a risk to trust. The same person can have a different job on Wednesday when a blocked project needs attention. That is why a living persona follows the situation, not only the person. For our fictional service, write: “When a new member opens the first task, they need to know what action matters now, so they can begin without asking staff to translate the instructions.” That sentence is a hypothesis. We have not interviewed a member. We can still use it to decide what to test and what to ask. Put a question mark beside the part you are least sure about. The mark is a reminder to listen, not a flaw in the card.

scenes.title: Build a smaller thing
scenes.narration: Once the job is visible, the build can get smaller. We do not need a complete onboarding platform to learn whether the first action is clear. We can make three versions of a first-task card: one with a short instruction, one with a guided step, and one that points to a person for help. Then we can ask what each version asks of the member and of the staff. The book's sequence matters. Shrink the question. Generate possible approaches without falling in love with the first one. Anchor the choice to strategy. Let AI help with an early draft if the inputs are safe. A quick draft is useful because it gives us something to inspect. It is not a user test. In the synthetic demonstration, I choose the guided step as the first prototype because it addresses the starting-point question from our decision file. I keep the other versions visible. If research shows that the instruction was already clear, I will change course. The purpose of the prototype is to put the assumption where we can see it.

scenes.title: Add evidence and uncertainty
scenes.narration: A living persona needs a record of where it came from. On the card, write the job, the context, the signal you observed, what remains uncertain, and the next validation question. Add a source and a review date. If this card is based on a real interview or a permitted product signal, cite the approved record without exposing the person in the course file. If it is a synthetic exercise, say so in the working evidence layer and leave “observed signal” blank. You can write a proposed signal to look for, but do not call it observed. Chapter Six is explicit that synthetic data can help generate hypotheses. It cannot replace real research or justify a high-stakes irreversible decision. This is especially easy to forget when a simulated person speaks in a convincing voice. A plausible quote is still invented. In our example, we do not know where actual members hesitate. The card should say that plainly. A useful persona can hold an unknown without collapsing. That is how it stays alive long enough to become more accurate.

scenes.title: Revisit the person, not the picture
scenes.narration: Imagine the test happens and the team learns that members understand the first instruction but pause because they cannot tell how long the task will take. That would change the card. The job might be less about finding the next action and more about knowing whether there is enough time to begin. I am making up that result to show how revision works; it is not a claim about a product or a customer. The important move is to date the update and keep the old assumption visible in the decision file. A persona that changes with evidence is more useful than a deck that stays beautiful while the work moves on. This does not require collecting every click or building a profile of every person. It requires consent, an approved source, and the discipline to separate what you observed from what you inferred. Ask whether the card helps you make today's product choice. If it cannot, revise the job or the question. The person behind the work deserves that care.

In the next lesson, the workshop will turn more raw feedback into traceable signal. For now, hold on to the small question. Build only enough to learn. Keep the card open to correction. scenes.title: A full inbox and an empty decision
scenes.narration: The comments keep coming. One person says the service is slow. Another says it is hard to start. Someone wants a reminder. The inbox is full, and the roadmap meeting is tomorrow. You can count the comments. You can paste them into a summary tool. Neither action tells you what to change. In Chapter Seven of Accelerated, discovery begins by asking what job people are trying to do when the trouble appears. That means keeping the original words close enough to check our interpretation. Imagine six notes from a membership service. Each has an ID, a moment, and a short comment. We can practice the method with them before applying it to interviews. The decision in our file is whether to improve the first task, add reminders, or investigate another barrier. Before grouping anything, write that decision above the notes. It gives the analysis a purpose. Then ask what evidence would make one of those paths more sensible than the others. A theme is useful only when it helps answer a real choice. The Signals plate is a map of that movement. We start with what people said, examine the situation behind it, and carry a narrower question into the next test.

scenes.title: Keep the raw words traceable
scenes.narration: Look at the first two notes. F zero one says, “I clicked begin and could not tell if anything happened.” F zero two says, “I came back later and could not find where I left off.” Both can sound like a request for speed. Their moments are different. The first person needs confirmation that an action worked. The second needs a reliable place to resume. If we label both “performance,” we may build the wrong fix. Give each row an input ID, the exact comment, the task underway, and a proposed job statement. Leave the job statement open to correction. We have not asked a person what they meant. The ID matters because a colleague can return to the note and challenge our reading. Add F zero three, who says the instructions are too long, and F zero four, who says a staff member explained the task in one sentence. Those notes may point to an instruction problem. They may also reflect different circumstances. Chapter Seven uses case structuring to move from anecdote to decision insight. Structuring is not sanding away the detail. It is a way to compare situations without losing the path back to the evidence. If a summary drops the IDs, the team loses that path. Keep the source beside every interpretation.

scenes.title: One complaint can hide several jobs
scenes.narration: The book has a useful warning here. In the “Just Make It Faster” case, a team received feedback that sounded like one performance complaint. When they examined the moment behind it, they found different needs: immediate confirmation after an action, current information from other people, and easier movement between views. The response to one need would not solve the others. I am treating that as a case from the book, not as a measurement of any tool we are showing today. In our example, F zero one belongs under confirmation. F zero two belongs under resume. F zero three and F zero four may belong under instruction clarity. Keep those groups provisional. Now read F zero five: “The first task loaded quickly, but I did not know whether it mattered.” That is a counterexample to the easy “speed” label and a clue about purpose. If we ignored it, we could make a fast page that still leaves someone stranded. F zero six says, “I started after the welcome email showed the first step.” That may support a clearer entry point, but one note cannot establish a general pattern. Ask what the people were trying to accomplish and where the workflow made that harder. The answer should lead toward a question the team can actually test.

scenes.title: A machine can cluster; a person must inspect
scenes.narration: Suppose a safe local draft groups F zero one through F zero five under “slow onboarding.” It sounds confident. Look at F zero five again. The page loaded quickly. The person did not understand why the task mattered. The draft has collapsed a meaning problem into a timing problem. Move that row back and record why. A tool can help sort a large set, suggest job statements, or point to questions the team has missed. In the book, that is an accelerator for discovery. The review still belongs to people who can check source, context, consent, and consequence. With private or restricted feedback, do not paste raw records into an external model without an approved data path. We can practice with the six notes in front of us. When your team uses its own feedback, keep consent, source, and context attached to each record. A polished cluster chart can make the room feel certain before the evidence is strong. Chapter Seven calls that danger feedback theater. The correction we just made is small, but it changes the possible product choice. We might test whether clearer purpose and confirmation help people begin. We would not claim that faster loading is the answer merely because the summary used the word “slow.”

scenes.title: Make one opportunity testable
scenes.narration: Our six notes support a question, not a verdict. Two notes point toward instruction clarity. One points toward action confirmation. One points toward resuming. One challenges the speed explanation, and one suggests an entry point that helped. That is too little to rank the needs of a real membership program. It is enough to practice the decision path. Write the proposed pattern as “people may hesitate at the first task when they cannot see what to do or why it matters.” Attach F zero three, F zero four, and F zero five. Keep F zero one visible as a competing confirmation need. The proposed decision is to test a clearer first-task card before committing to a reminder system. The next step could be a short observation with participants who agree to take part. First, a team walkthrough can catch obvious confusion in the card. Then participant evidence can show how people actually behave. The book's discovery loop moves through collecting, synthesizing, prioritizing, validating, and archiving learning. We are at the synthesis step. We have not validated an outcome. Link this ledger to the living persona card from the last lesson, then write the question that would change the decision. If members understand the card yet still hesitate, we need to look elsewhere.

scenes.title: Leave room for the contrary note
scenes.narration: Pause and code the six notes. Put each ID beside its raw wording. Add the moment, a possible job, and the group you would test. Mark at least one note that resists your favorite explanation. Then write a pattern in cautious language and name the decision it could affect. Resume when someone else could trace your recommendation back to the input rows and see where you might be wrong. If you use your own material, choose records you have permission to share. It carries the original signal forward without pretending a small sample is a finding. The temptation is to end with a crisp theme and move immediately to a feature. Stay one step longer. Ask whose job this describes, who may be absent from the notes, and what observation would challenge it. You can make a decision under uncertainty as long as the uncertainty travels with it. In the next lesson, this proposed choice enters a roadmap and then a product requirements document. If the source disappears along that path, the team may build a polished answer to a question nobody asked. Keep the ID in view.

scenes.title: Three cards on the wall
scenes.narration: There are three cards on the wall. Add a reminder. Rewrite the first task. Give staff a dashboard. Every card has someone who can make a case for it. The meeting could become a contest of confidence, and the team could leave with a list that feels balanced but teaches little. Put the feedback ledger from the last lesson beside the cards. F zero three, F zero four, and F zero five suggest that the first task may need clearer direction and purpose. F zero one suggests another need: confirmation that an action worked. None of those six notes proves a solution. They do give us a reason to ask a better roadmap question. Chapter Eight says to turn features into bets about customer and business outcomes. A bet states what we believe will change, for whom, and how we will know. For the membership service, write: “If a clearer first-task card helps new members understand the next action, more of them should begin that task without staff translating the instruction.” That is a hypothesis, not a promise. The other two cards stay on the wall. We need a reason to choose now and a signal that would bring an alternative back. The roadmap should carry both, in words the team can remember.

scenes.title: Choose with criteria and keep the alternatives

scenes.title: The PRD opens with the change we seek
scenes.narration: Now the bet enters a product requirements document. A blank template can make a team start with controls and screens. For this exercise, begin one line earlier: “A new member opens the first task and cannot tell what action matters or why.” Under that line, link the ledger IDs. scenes.title: Ask someone to explain the handoff back
scenes.narration: Before anyone builds, ask a teammate to explain the bet back in their own words. “We want to see whether a clearer first task helps a new member begin. We are testing one card, and we will observe the starting moment.” Good. Then ask what happens if the member presses begin and loses connection. Does the interface say the action worked? Can the person safely try again? F zero one already warned us that confirmation may matter. A document that says “show success” without defining this case leaves a real decision to chance. A person who will build or support the change needs to review the meaning. Add an acceptance check: after a successful start, the member sees a clear state; after a failed attempt, the card says what happened and what to do next. The team may refine that check during design. Record who made the decision and why. This is a small handoff, yet it contains the same failure mode as a large program: the source question can disappear while the document becomes more detailed. Keep it visible at the top.

scenes.title: Keep a living line from evidence to measure
scenes.narration: Imagine the team tests the card and finds that people understand the action but still cannot tell whether they have finished it. Imagine that result for a moment. The next move may be better completion feedback rather than more instruction. Update the PRD and the trace card. Chapter Nine's living document is how decisions made in review, design, and development remain visible to the people who were not in every conversation. The roadmap should change with that learning as well. It is a story about the outcome we are trying to move and the bets we are willing to test, not a schedule that erases its own history. Our trace card has a source: the L05 ledger. It has a current decision: test the first-task guide. It has an owner and a limited scope. It names the exclusions. The measure is whether a participant can identify and begin the intended action in a planned test, with the observation method stated before the result. We have not measured it yet. A clean trace lets a future teammate ask why this work entered the plan and see an answer they can challenge.

scenes.title: Draw the line all the way through

scenes.title: The quarter is full
scenes.narration: The quarter is full before it starts. A new first-task card is due in two weeks. A reminder system is penciled in after that. Someone has promised a dashboard by the end of the month. The schedule looks responsible, but the team still cannot answer a basic question: why do new members hesitate at the first task? Write the outcome we seek at the top: a member can understand and begin the first task without staff translating it. Under that, write what we need to learn first. Is the barrier unclear instruction, weak confirmation, or something else? A feature date can tell us when work will ship. A learning checkpoint tells us when we will inspect what the work taught us and decide whether to continue. Let us build two checkpoints for the membership service we have been following. We are planning the questions before any member responds. Keep the dates visible, but make each date earn a question. Otherwise a team can meet every deadline while its original uncertainty travels untouched into the next quarter.

scenes.title: Checkpoint one: diagnose before expanding
scenes.narration: Checkpoint one is a diagnosis. The question is whether new members understand the first instruction and the purpose of the task. The method could be a small observation of the starting moment, paired with the original feedback IDs. The owner schedules the review before a larger build begins. If participants can explain the action but cannot tell whether pressing begin worked, confirmation becomes the stronger next question. If they cannot explain what the task is for, the instruction and purpose deserve attention. If both are clear, we reopen the problem instead of forcing one of our planned features through. Write those possible adjustments now. This is what the book means by making learning a deliverable. The team is accountable for running a sound test, reviewing the evidence, and recording a decision. It cannot honestly guarantee the customer outcome before seeing what happens. Keep the method proportionate to the question. A team walkthrough can catch confusing copy before a participant sees it. It cannot tell us how members behave. For that, invite people through a consented research process and keep their notes where your team protects customer information. scenes.narration: Checkpoint two follows only if the first review supports the instruction hypothesis. The team tests the smaller first-task card against the existing version in a planned study. scenes.title: Sam's team changes its question
scenes.narration: Chapter Eleven tells a story about Sam and her team. A junior product manager brings an unfinished idea into the team channel. Sam expects to step in and shape it. Instead, colleagues ask what customer outcome the idea addresses, whether the job has been validated, and what they would learn by testing it. scenes.title: A failed test still changes the plan
scenes.narration: The book gives Sam's team a test that does not support the feature they built. They try document previews, expecting people to find the right file faster. The review points them toward a different need: better search. The team records the learning and changes direction. What matters for us is how the team responded when the test challenged its original bet. Look at the sequence. They stated a hypothesis. They chose a signal and review point. They inspected the result. Then they asked what the result meant for the user's job. A low number by itself would not tell them whether the feature was hidden, unwanted, or solving the wrong task. The follow-up conversation mattered. Apply that discipline to our membership example. If the first-task card gets used but members still need staff help, do not declare success because the card was opened. If people never reach it, check the entry path before judging its wording. If the instruction helps but the next step fails, write that down. The team can hold delivery accountable and still let evidence change the next bet. That is a practical promise to the people who have to live with the roadmap.

scenes.title: A dashboard can look healthy
scenes.narration: The dashboard is green. More people are opening the page. The team celebrates, then support hears that members still cannot finish the first task. A rising activity line did not answer the question we were trying to solve. Chapter Twelve tells a version of this failure: a dashboard looked healthy while the product was missing the customer outcome. The point is to choose a measure that belongs to the decision. In the membership service example, the business may care about sustained participation. A member cares about getting started without confusion. The team can first observe whether a person identifies and begins the intended action. Those are different levels of the metrics ladder in the book: business value, customer value, and near-term traction. The lower step does not automatically cause the upper one. We need to test the connection. If page opens rise while people still ask staff what to do, the green chart is a warning, not a win. Write the customer behavior in a sentence before selecting a metric. For this lesson, it is: a new member understands the first task and starts it without translation from staff. Now ask what observation would support or challenge that sentence. A useful measure can be counted or described consistently. It also needs a definition that another person can apply to the same event. We will put that definition into the learning plan before seeing any result.

scenes.title: Define the measure and its guardrail
scenes.narration: Define a successful start before the test begins. For a moderated session, that might mean the participant can point to the intended action, explain its purpose in their own words, and begin without staff explaining the instruction. The numerator is the number of observed participants who meet that definition. The denominator is the number of eligible participants who reach the first-task moment. Record exclusions before the session, such as an interrupted test or a technical outage. A second observer should be able to check the same notes and understand the count. That measure is close to the behavior we seek. It still cannot tell us everything. Ask the participant where they hesitated and what they expected to happen. That qualitative note may show whether the copy, confirmation, or task itself is the problem. Chapter Twelve also warns about destructive metric pairs. We could maximize time spent on the first task while saying we want people to begin quickly. Longer time might mean careful engagement, or it might mean confusion. We need the context before celebrating either direction. Pair the successful-start measure with a guardrail: the person should not have to ask staff to rescue the flow or repeat an action because the state is unclear. A planned measurement cannot promise a conversion or retention lift. The definition is a proposed measurement instrument; the outcome remains unknown until a test is run and reviewed.

scenes.title: The first five components establish the bet
scenes.narration: Chapter Thirteen gives the learning plan ten components. The first five establish what we are testing. One: business problem and customer outcome. Our example names the friction at the first task and the member's need to begin with confidence. We will not claim a business lift from this small exercise. Two: target persona or cohort. Use the living persona card from lesson four: a new member at the first-task moment. Add the source and the uncertainty so the card stays honest about what we know. Three: hypothesis statement. We believe a clearer first-task card, for a new member in that moment, will help them identify and begin the intended action without staff translation. Four: experiment scope. Specify the test setting, who is eligible, how long observation lasts, and which version of the card they see. Exclude the reminder system and the rest of onboarding. Five: metrics and success criteria. Use the successful-start definition we just wrote, the qualitative hesitation notes, and a threshold set by the actual study owner before data arrives. These fields belong together. If the cohort is vague, a clean metric can mislead. If the outcome is vague, a detailed experiment may only test whether a screen is clickable. On this worksheet, leave the actual threshold marked for owner decision. That blank is honest. The team must fill it before running a real test; it must not choose a convenient number after looking at results.

scenes.title: The next five decide what happens afterward
scenes.narration: The next five components keep the test from ending at a chart. Six: timing and review strategy. Decide when the team checks for setup problems, when it reads the observations, and when it makes the next decision. Seven: triggers and tripwires. State what pattern would support continuing, what would require revision, and what would make the team stop or investigate harm. For our example, repeated confusion or unclear failure states would pause expansion even if some people begin. The exact numerical threshold is still an owner decision before the test. Eight: pivot options. If members understand the card but never return, investigate the reminder path. If they reach the card but cannot tell whether the action worked, test confirmation. Those are possible branches, not findings. Nine: future state path. If the small test supports the hypothesis and passes its guardrail, name the next bounded question rather than announcing a full rollout. Perhaps the team tests the same instruction with another eligible group. Ten: hypothesis backlog. Save the original belief, result, learning, owner, and date so the next team does not start from an empty page. That is the book's order. The plan carries both a decision and a memory of how the decision was made. A result can be positive, negative, or inconclusive. The point is that each route has a responsible next action already visible before the room gets attached to one answer.

scenes.title: Walk the plan against two possible results
scenes.narration: Before there is any data, walk the plan through two possible results. In the first, participants understand the action and begin, but several say the confirmation is unclear. The successful-start measure may look promising. The guardrail tells us the work is not finished. We record the uncertainty and test feedback after the action before broadening the scope. In the second, participants cannot explain why the task matters. That result challenges the instruction itself. The team revises the purpose statement and tests again. These are imagined branches. Both results are possibilities, not findings. Notice how the metric definition changes the conversation. “More opens” would let both situations hide behind activity. “Understands and begins without translation” brings the actual behavior into view. The qualitative note explains why a count moved and what it cannot tell us. If the sample is too small, unrepresentative, or interrupted, mark the outcome inconclusive and choose a better test. Chapter Twelve asks us to tie measures to hypotheses and prepare to be wrong. Chapter Thirteen gives us a place to record that preparation. The worksheet is useful only if a team can follow it when the answer is inconvenient. Keep the threshold, exclusions, and branch choices dated before the test. Then, after a real review, record what happened and what the team decided. Do not rewrite the original bet to make the result look inevitable afterward to anyone.

scenes.title: The slow no
scenes.narration: You bring a careful recommendation into the room. The research is sound. The test plan has a measure and a stop condition. Someone asks about a competing priority. Engineering asks whose work will move. A person who was not in the meeting raises a concern afterward. The answer becomes, “Let's revisit this next quarter.” Chapter Fourteen opens with a version of that slow no. Its lesson is practical: the evidence may be strong while the path to a decision is weak. People in the room have different information, responsibilities, and memories of the last failed bet. A leader may see budget risk. An engineer may see a promised platform change. A support lead may see another workflow they will have to explain. Before you call those reactions resistance, find out what each person is trying to protect. Return to the learning plan you wrote in lesson eight. You know the customer behavior you hope to change, the test you propose, and what would stop it. Now write the actual decision you need from this room. Is it permission to run the small test, funding for a larger build, or agreement to stop something else? Those are different asks. For our fictional membership service, the ask is a bounded test of a clearer first-task card. We will map the people and conversations that would make that test responsible.

scenes.title: Build the argument before the deck
scenes.narration: Chapter Fourteen names a Strategic Argument Blueprint. It has six parts, and the order matters. First, the problem: new members struggle to identify the first action without staff translation. That is a hypothesis for this exercise, not a measured customer finding. Second, the opportunity: a clearer entry might reduce that burden and help members begin. We do not assign a revenue figure to that possibility. Third, options: clarify the card, test a guided introduction, or hold the current flow until we learn more. Fourth, the recommendation: test the smallest card change because it gives us an answer with limited build effort. Fifth, tradeoffs: somebody must prepare the card, observe sessions, and delay another small task. Put that cost in the open. Sixth, outcome: the learning plan defines what a successful start looks like and what confusion would stop expansion. This is an argument for a decision, not a list of features. The same six fields can fit a short brief. In an email, lead with the decision requested. In a live meeting, let people see the problem and then the options. In a one-to-one conversation, listen for a missing criterion before polishing the deck. The blueprint does not guarantee agreement. It makes the choice and its cost visible enough for people to challenge honestly.

scenes.title: Map roles and behavior
scenes.narration: Chapter Fifteen says an org chart is a start, but it will not show every decision path. Its first stakeholder lens is role type. A decision-maker can approve or stop the work. An influencer shapes that person's view. A gatekeeper controls access, capacity, or information. A champion advocates. A skeptic asks hard questions. A blocker may actively oppose the idea. One person can occupy more than one role, and the label is a working hypothesis, not a verdict on character. On the synthetic card, a service director can authorize the test. An operations lead controls the staff time needed to observe it. A front-line worker knows where members lose the thread. A finance partner wants to know what the test displaces. We use fictional roles because this exercise needs a map, not anyone's private contact history. Add behavior next. Who tends to ask for customer evidence? Who trusts the team that must build the change? Who remembers an earlier rollout that increased support work? The answer changes what you bring into a conversation. It should not change the underlying evidence. Give the operations lead the observation burden and exclusions. Give the service director the decision and stop condition. Ask the front-line worker whether our assumed friction even matches what they see. If they say no, revise the hypothesis before the meeting. Mapping makes you more accurate about the work and the people who carry it.

scenes.title: Use the book's power-interest grid
scenes.narration: The book's third lens is a power-interest grid. High power and high interest means manage closely. High power and low interest means keep satisfied. Low power and high interest means keep informed. Low power and low interest means monitor. Those are the book's four labels. Draw the two axes and place our four fictional roles for this one decision. The service director has authority and cares about the member experience, so manage closely. The operations lead can withhold observation time and has a strong interest in the workflow, so manage closely too. The front-line worker may have little formal power but deep interest and useful evidence: keep informed and invite their challenge early. The finance partner may have approval influence but only intermittent interest: keep satisfied with a clear cost and review point. This placement is provisional. A policy change could move finance into the center. A staff member who has the director's trust may carry more informal influence than their title suggests. Ask the people involved, then update the map. Do not use the grid to silence people with less formal power. They may know the customer burden first. The visual helps plan communication; it does not decide whose knowledge counts. Put an objection beside each role and one piece of evidence or question that would help. If you cannot name what would change a person's mind, have a conversation before sending a finished pitch.

scenes.title: Sequence quiet conversations
scenes.narration: The book calls the pre-meeting work Shuttle Diplomacy. Learn the decision criteria before a deck hardens around one answer. Start with the person who will do the observation. Ask the operations lead what time the test would take and which staffing constraint would make it unsafe. Next, ask the front-line worker whether the proposed card addresses the moment they see members hesitate. If the answer is another problem entirely, record it. Then ask the finance partner what cost or displaced work they would expect to see in the brief. Finally, give the service director the revised options and the specific decision requested. These are conversations with real stakes in a real project. Here they are a fictional sequence for practice, not a report that outreach happened. Keep confidential notes out of a rehearsal tool. If you rehearse objections with AI, use a synthetic brief and treat the output as questions to examine, never as that person's opinion. Chapter Fourteen recommends rehearsing pushback. The stronger version of that advice is to let people correct your understanding when you can speak with them. Update the decision file after each conversation: concern raised, evidence supporting it, what remains unknown, and whether the proposal changed. A meeting can focus on the live choice instead of surprising people with costs that were visible all week.

scenes.title: The proposal that did not land
scenes.narration: A proposal can be right about the customer and still arrive in the wrong form. The team sees the research. Finance sees an unpriced commitment. Engineering sees work that may displace a promised upgrade. The person presenting keeps adding evidence, but no one has named the decision that each listener is being asked to carry. Chapter Sixteen describes that kind of meeting. It also returns to the decision theater: stakeholders have authority, fears, and limited attention. Our membership-service example is fictional. We want to test a clearer first-task card, and the map from lesson nine tells us who needs to hear the case. Before changing the message, hold the evidence steady. We have a hypothesis about confusion, a proposed observation method, and a stop condition. We do not have a measured lift or a real approval. Write that distinction at the top of the brief. Then ask what each person must decide. The service director decides whether the test is worth running. Operations decides whether staff can observe it safely. Finance needs the time and cost bound. One proposal can answer all three without pretending that their risks are identical. That is where influence begins.

scenes.title: Keep the claim, change the emphasis

scenes.title: Name the option we are passing over
scenes.narration: Chapter Sixteen uses a notification-settings case. An initial request for granular controls did not land. The revised case made the underlying problem, options, and tradeoffs easier to judge. We are borrowing that decision structure, not its reported results. In our exercise, option one is to rewrite the first-task card and observe whether members understand and begin. Option two is a guided introduction by staff. That may help now, but it may also increase staff burden. Option three is to defer the change while we gather better evidence about where confusion starts. The recommendation is option one, a small test with an explicit stop condition. The other options remain on the page. If the card is clear but people still do not return, the next question may concern reminders or motivation. If the instruction is misunderstood, we revise it. If operations cannot support the observation, we change the test plan before asking for approval. The brief should name what we are not doing and why. That gives a decision owner a real choice. It also protects the team from turning a narrow learning bet into an unlimited promise after the meeting.

scenes.title: State the tradeoff without theater
scenes.narration: Tradeoffs are where a polished pitch often turns vague. Say exactly what this test would take. Someone must write two versions of the card, recruit eligible participants through an approved process, observe the first-task moment, and review the notes. The team must decide which small task moves to make room. We do not have a credible cost figure in this synthetic case, so the real owner must fill it in before a real approval. The test excludes a reminder redesign and the rest of onboarding. The decision file already has a measure, a qualitative companion, and a stop condition. Put their owners and dates beside the ask. If the guardrail shows that people need staff rescue or cannot tell whether an action worked, the team pauses expansion. If observation is too thin to support a choice, record that too. Chapter Sixteen's pitch checklist asks for the problem, evidence, options, tradeoffs, and an ask. The ask here is permission to run a bounded learning test. It is not permission to launch the redesigned experience to everyone. A clear limit gives the decision owner a safer way to say yes, revise, or decline. It also gives the team a way to know what was actually approved.

scenes.title: Rehearse a real objection
scenes.narration: Imagine operations says, “We cannot spare staff to watch a long session.” Do not answer by repeating why the customer problem matters. Ask which part of the observation creates the burden. Could the test use fewer sessions, a shorter window, or an existing research appointment? If none is feasible, stop and redesign the test. Imagine finance says, “Why should this displace the dashboard task?” Show the explicit alternative, the staff time, and the learning question that each option answers. Ask what evidence would make the tradeoff acceptable. An AI rehearsal with a synthetic brief can suggest possible objections, but it cannot report what operations or finance actually thinks. Only their answers can do that. Chapter Sixteen treats pre-meeting conversations as part of influence. The useful outcome is not a script that defeats every objection. It is a proposal that has absorbed the right ones. Record the objection in the decision file, with its source and date. Mark whether the response changes scope, timing, owner, or the recommendation itself. If you find that the test would burden the very staff it is meant to help, that is a reason to pause. Responsible influence leaves room for the other person to improve the choice.

scenes.title: Deliver the 90-second decision brief
scenes.narration: Pause and draft a ninety-second recommendation for one decision owner on your map. Open with the decision you need. State the problem and what evidence actually supports it. Give the preferred small option and one credible alternative. Name its cost, the work it displaces, who owns the test, and the date of review. End with the result that would make you stop or change course. Resume when you can say the whole thing aloud without a slide. For our fictional service director, it might sound like this: “We propose a small test of the first-task card. The current friction is a hypothesis. We will observe whether eligible new members understand and begin without staff translation. Operations must confirm the time and recruitment path. A guided introduction remains the alternative. If participants remain confused or need staff rescue, we revise before expansion. We will bring the observations back on the agreed date.” That brief does not claim success in advance. Write a second opening for the operations lead, using the same facts and their concern. Then answer one final question: what would change your mind? If the answer is “nothing,” revisit the learning plan. A decision brief should make learning possible, even when the answer is inconvenient.

scenes.title: A shorter meeting
scenes.narration: In Chapter Seventeen, Sam arrives at a roadmap meeting that feels different. The team has already gathered feedback, translated it into a question, and prepared a learning choice. The meeting can spend its time on the decision. Sam is a character in the book's story, not a member of a team we are showing live. What changed was the work before the meeting. Evidence had a place to arrive. A plan had a review point. A failed test could be discussed without scrambling to explain it away. Think about your last meeting that started with everyone retelling the same customer problem. How much time went into finding the latest notes? How much into arguing over which number was current? Shorter meetings are not the goal by themselves. The useful change is that the team can see what it knows, what it tried, and what it will decide next. Your decision file already holds a source ledger, a learning plan, and a map of the decision room. Today we connect those pages. We will ask where a signal enters, who checks it, how a test is chosen, who decides, and where the result is kept for the next person. That is the quiet infrastructure behind the changed meeting.

scenes.title: Trace the failed test
scenes.narration: The book gives Sam a test that fails. The team's learning plan had already said what result would make them change course, so the failure did not have to become a debate about whether the work counted. They could ask what the result meant and choose the next question. Notice what that requires. The original hypothesis must still be visible. The trigger cannot be rewritten after the result. Someone must inspect the evidence rather than accept a summary alone. The decision and its reason need to survive the meeting. In our membership exercise, imagine the new first-task card is tested and people still ask staff for help. That is a conditional branch, not a result. The team might learn that the instruction is unclear, or that the task itself is unfamiliar. The observation notes would need to distinguish those explanations. If participants understand the card but cannot tell whether the action worked, confirmation becomes the next test. If recruitment fails, the study is inconclusive. The file should preserve all three routes without pretending that one happened. Sam's story shows an operating habit: a team can be wrong about a solution and still be disciplined about learning. The record is what lets the next meeting start beyond the last one.

scenes.title: Connect signal, insight, test, decision
scenes.narration: Chapter Eighteen moves from scattered tools to a connected system. Its arrow sequence begins with signal, then insight, test, decision, and repeatable momentum. A signal is a traceable observation, such as a set of first-task notes with source IDs. An insight is an interpretation: perhaps members cannot tell which action starts the service. That interpretation still needs a counterexample and a person willing to challenge it. A test turns the interpretation into a question that can be answered. The learning plan specifies who participates, what counts, and when the result is reviewed. A decision says what the team will do in light of that evidence. Repeatable momentum means the next person can find the record and use it without rebuilding the whole argument. In our synthetic workflow, feedback note F04 reaches the ledger. The reviewer groups it with similar notes, preserves the contrary case, and writes a proposed job. The owner chooses a small card test. The result, when one exists, returns to the decision file with a date and next move. This path is still a proposal until a team names its owners and review gates. Draw each arrow only after naming its input, owner, and output. A line between boxes is not a handoff unless someone can tell when the work crosses it and what happens when it does not.

scenes.title: Put a person at the review gate
scenes.narration: The book names tools that can collect, translate, and route information. The trap is to connect them and call the system complete. If an AI summary misreads a member's sentence, faster routing only spreads the mistake. In this course, automation may move an approved note into a ledger, flag a possible pattern, or remind an owner that a review date has arrived. A person checks the raw source, contrary evidence, privacy boundary, and decision consequence before a proposed insight becomes a team commitment. That review gate needs a named owner and a visible way to reject or correct the suggestion. For the fictional membership service, a coordinator could review the source IDs before the pattern reaches the product owner. If the note contains private information, it stays in the protected research system and only an approved summary travels onward. The book's minimum viable stack is about connecting the work, not collecting every tool on a shelf. Choose the smallest path your team can actually maintain. Write what happens when the reviewer is unavailable. Does the item wait, move to another authorized owner, or expire? A silent automated approval would change the decision boundary. The loop should make that boundary plain enough for a new teammate to follow.

scenes.title: Give the next person the memory
scenes.narration: Imagine joining this work six weeks later. You should be able to answer three questions without searching through a long chat. What did the team believe? What did it observe? What did it decide? The record needs the original hypothesis, the test version, the source links, the measure and guardrail, the reviewer, the decision date, and the next owner. If the evidence is inconclusive, write that plainly. If a later team repeats the test in a different setting, it should keep the earlier result rather than overwrite it. Chapter Eighteen calls the real goal a system that remembers. Memory here is operational: it keeps a small decision from becoming a rumor. Sam's changed meeting in Chapter Seventeen depends on this kind of continuity. In our exercise, a record might say the first-task card remains untested because observation capacity was unavailable. That is not a failure dressed up as success. It is a clear state and a next action. Another possible record could say the test ran but the result is awaiting human review. Neither should be described as an outcome. Keep source links in the authorized system, not on a public slide. The audience-facing card can show the shape of the record with fictional values.

scenes.title: A pile of feedback is not a job
scenes.narration: The feedback pile is growing again. One note says, “I could not tell where to start.” Another asks for a reminder. A third says the task looked complete but the page gave no confirmation. These are fictional member comments carried forward from our earlier exercise. If we group them too quickly under “improve onboarding,” we lose the difference between finding an action, remembering it, and knowing it worked. Chapter Nineteen introduces ClientQ as a way to translate messy feedback into jobs. The book case gives us a method for examining the notes. The useful discipline is to keep every proposed job tied to the source note that suggested it. Start with what the person was trying to do, the context in which it mattered, and the outcome they wanted. Then ask whether another note points to the same job or a different one. A cluster can be convenient and still be wrong. We also need the contrary note that challenges the pattern. In the decision file, F01 through F06 remain visible beside any synthesis. If one sentence is ambiguous, mark it for a human follow-up rather than turn it into an invented certainty. Today we will write a job card and then test its weak spots with simulation. The source stays visible throughout.

scenes.title: Translate without inventing
scenes.narration: Chapter Nineteen makes a crucial distinction: ClientQ processes data; it does not create the underlying customer experience. Work through one fictional note. F01 says the member does not know which action begins the service. The context is the first visit after joining. A possible job is: “Help me identify the first useful action when I arrive, so I can begin without asking staff to translate the page.” That sentence is our interpretation of the note, not a verbatim customer quote. Write F01 beside it. F03 may support the same job, but inspect its wording before adding it. A note about missing confirmation may instead become a separate job: “Help me know whether the action succeeded so I can move on with confidence.” Do not combine them just because they occur on the same screen. The book also shows an outcome-style formulation, such as reducing time spent searching when a task is urgent. We can use that grammar without pretending to have measured importance or satisfaction. If an AI assistant suggests a job, compare it against each source. Ask what word in the original note supports the proposed context and outcome. Where support is thin, label the job provisional. The next step is a question for a person or an observation, not a confident backlog priority.

scenes.title: ClientQ is a book case, not proof of our workflow
scenes.narration: The book calls ClientQ a translator for customer language. It describes clustering comments, extracting jobs, and moving possible opportunities toward a hypothesis backlog. That is a case in the book. Our six-card exercise is separate. The cards in this exercise are imagined member notes, separate from observed research. A third category would be actual research collected with permission. Keep these three categories apart when you present a job statement. In a real project, preserve the original note, source date, consent and access rules, the interpretation, and who reviewed it. If a team reports frequency, the count must come from the actual source set and its defined unit, such as people or comments. Do not invent a percentage because several cards on a training slide look similar. The book's warning is clear: synthesis cannot replace talking with people. A pattern extracted from comments may help choose which conversation to have next. It cannot tell us by itself whether a proposed screen solves the need. For our decision file, put the job card beside the first-task hypothesis from earlier lessons. Ask whether the hypothesis still matches the job. If the problem is knowing whether an action worked, a clearer first-task invitation may be the wrong test. Correcting the question before building is progress.

scenes.title: Simulate objections without borrowing authority
scenes.narration: Chapter Twenty introduces SudoPoll, a book case for synthetic persona reactions. It can suggest objections to a concept, but its output is a simulation. It is not a customer interview, a survey, or a statistically valid preference count. Imagine asking how a new member might respond to two versions of the first-task card. One simulated response says the shorter card is easier to scan but does not explain what happens after the click. Another says the detailed card feels safer but is too much to read at the doorway. Both reactions are invented for this teaching example. They are useful as questions: do real members need a clearer outcome promise, a stronger confirmation, or less text? They are not votes for one design. The book names three limits around emotional nuance, cultural context, and behavioral prediction. Those limits matter especially when the service touches trust or access. A model can draw on patterns it has seen; it cannot stand in for the people the organization serves. Put a visible Simulation label on every generated reaction. Keep the proposed objection beside the exact concept version that produced it. If the model imagines a concern you had not considered, add it to a validation plan. Do not claim that real customers raised it.

scenes.title: Set the real-world checkpoint
scenes.narration: The simulation points to two questions, not two answers. First: can an eligible new member explain the first action before beginning it? Second: after acting, can they tell whether it worked? Put each beside a real observation method. The research owner can watch an approved session, ask the person what they expect, and record the observed hesitation. The team must decide in advance who is eligible, how the notes are protected, what the measure means, and what would stop expansion. If the stakes rise toward a launch decision, simulated reactions are no longer enough. Chapter Twenty says to graduate to real people when behavior matters or cultural and emotional context could change the interpretation. In our fictional case, the launch choice stays blocked until actual evidence is reviewed. Even if every simulated persona likes the card, the team has learned only that the card survived a rehearsal. We can use that rehearsal to improve the research questions. We cannot use it to fill the result field of the ten-component plan. Keep the job statement and its original source notes in the file. Keep the simulation output in a separate, clearly marked section. At the review, compare both with what real people did and said. If reality contradicts the simulation, the real observation changes the course.

scenes.title: Finish the two cards
scenes.narration: Pause and make two cards. On the first, write one job statement from the synthetic feedback bundle. scenes.title: Flat is a question, not a verdict
scenes.narration: Picture a Monday meeting. The dashboard is flat. Someone says the product needs a pivot, and the room starts naming new features before anyone has agreed what is stuck. In Chapter Twenty-One, Sam faces that pressure and opens StratQuest. This is a book story. Our membership-service example is a separate teaching exercise. Its numbers are intentionally blank because we have observed no customer result for this exercise. Start with four possible constraints. Is the customer job poorly understood? Is the product hard to use? Does the way people pay conflict with when they receive value? Or is the offer reaching the wrong buyer? Each explanation points to a different test. A flat chart alone cannot distinguish them. Bring forward the job and evidence gap from the last lesson. If the job is unverified, price changes may only make an unclear service cheaper. If the job is clear and people use the service in bursts, the model deserves scrutiny. Write the assumption that would make a model change sensible. Put its source beside it. A strategic conversation gets better when the room can see which claim came from a person, which came from a record, and which is still a guess. We are diagnosing before we commit resources. A useful diagnosis can also rule out the most attractive explanation. Record the rejected explanation and the evidence that weakened it. That line may save the team from revisiting the same argument next month.

scenes.title: Compare the book's alternatives
scenes.narration: StratQuest is the name of the book's guided strategy case. The chapter compares usage-based pricing, a seasonal freemium upgrade, and a professional-services hybrid for a subscription problem. Those are its alternatives, not a recommendation for every business. Put the options side by side. Usage-based pricing can align payment with active use, but billing and cash flow become more variable. A free tier can lower the first commitment, but a generous free offer may never lead to the job people will pay to complete. Services can bring expert help close to the customer, but delivery capacity becomes part of the model. For our fictional membership service, borrow the comparison method, not the book's results. Ask who pays, when value arrives, what work staff must do, and what would make the change reversible. Keep a fourth column for the current model. The current choice is an alternative too; it carries costs and deserves a fair test. A model is a set of operating promises. It changes invoices, service rhythms, support, and the customer's expectations. If we cannot explain those consequences, we are not ready to announce a pivot. We are ready to ask a better question. Keep this comparison on one page. If the proposal requires a second system, a new contract, or more staff time, write that requirement in the same row as its promised benefit.

scenes.title: Design the smallest strategic test
scenes.narration: The fourth StratQuest session turns a preferred option into a test. In the book case, a cohort compares a flexible price with the existing subscription. We will not copy its percentages into our exercise or promise the same outcome. Suppose our fictional membership service wonders whether a shorter commitment would help new members begin. A first test could be a concept interview with approved participants, followed by a small, consented offer test only if the organization can fulfill the new terms. Decide what evidence would support the idea and what would make you stop. Conversion alone is too narrow. Check whether people understand the offer, whether staff can deliver it, and whether the economics remain viable. Put the test in the ten-component learning plan from Lesson Eight. Name the owner and the date before seeing any result. If the test could affect billing or access, a responsible operator reviews the terms before any live exposure. For this workshop, the card remains fictional. The point is the decision structure: one model assumption, one bounded test, one measure of customer value, one measure of operating cost, and a condition for changing course. The test should reduce uncertainty without making a promise the team cannot keep. Make the stop condition observable. A vague sense that the test is not working will be hard to use when the team has already invested effort and hopes the result improves.

scenes.title: Make the future concept explainable
scenes.narration: A model choice can sound logical inside the team and confusing outside it. Chapter Twenty-Two brings in VisionScope and MarketCraft. The book presents VisionScope as a way to articulate an early concept, including a future-facing announcement and hard questions. MarketCraft pressures the positioning across audiences. These are named book cases; we are not demonstrating a live product. Write a one-hundred-word explanation of the proposed membership change. Begin with the person's situation. Say what they could do differently, when they would see value, and what the organization would need to provide. Leave out imaginary testimonials and performance figures. The book's collaboration-feature example is useful because different departments pictured different products under the same phrase. A clear narrative makes those disagreements visible early. If one reader imagines a self-service tool and another imagines a staffed program, the draft has revealed an unresolved operating choice. Put a question beside each contested sentence. The narrative is a test object, not a launch announcement. Its value is that a customer or colleague can point to the part they doubt. Now the team can learn whether the concept is understood before investing in the full build. Read the concept to someone outside the project. Ask them to explain it back in their own words. Their confusion may expose a decision your team has quietly postponed.

scenes.title: A good plan meets a skeptical room
scenes.narration: The plan is ready. The evidence ledger is organized. Yet the first person hearing the recommendation asks about delivery cost, while the second asks who benefits. Chapter Twenty-Three calls this the last-mile problem and introduces Persuasive Business Case GPT. That is a book case, not a live demonstration here. Another represents the people who use the service. They need different openings, but the underlying claim and source record must remain the same. Write the decision in one sentence before adjusting the pitch. Are we asking to run a bounded test, approve a permanent model, or fund a full rollout? A polished argument can blur those requests. State the smallest actual decision. Then check the evidence column. Which facts come from observed behavior? Which costs are estimates? Which reactions were only simulated? We can tailor the order in which we present them. We cannot promote an assumption into a fact because the room prefers certainty.
