scenes.title: Hold the source steady
scenes.narration: The chapter's dashboard example shows how a business case changes with the audience. It is a story in the book; we will not repeat its outcome figures as current evidence. For our fictional test, the operations pitch begins with the workload: what staff would have to record, when they would review it, and which service promise remains unchanged. If the wording becomes stronger than the record, weaken it or seek evidence. This discipline protects trust. People will disagree about which risk matters most. They should not have to wonder whether they heard two versions of the truth. The question for the pitch is simple: what must this particular person decide, and what can the source actually support?

scenes.title: Name the cost and rejected option
scenes.narration: A persuasive pitch must make the cost visible. The shorter-commitment test could require staff training, a clearer cancellation path, and a way to handle pauses. Those are possible operating requirements in our fictional exercise, not measured costs. Put them on the card before the recommendation. Add the option to keep the current model and the option to defer until the job is verified. Why test now? Because the evidence suggests a particular mismatch worth examining. Why a bounded test? Because the economics and user experience still have open questions. The book's pre-pitch workflow asks for objections before the meeting, when they can still improve the plan. It also identifies a common mistake: asking an assistant to make a weak case sound strong. Do the reverse. Ask which sentence needs a source, which cost is missing, and which stakeholder can block the test for a good reason. Then revise the proposal. If the answer is that the test cannot be run safely or fairly, say so. A decision brief is useful when it helps the group choose, including a decision to wait.

scenes.title: Rehearse objections as rehearsal
scenes.narration: A pre-pitch exercise can surface objections before the room does. Give the proposed test and its evidence to a reviewer. Ask them to challenge the weakest assumption, the delivery burden, and the risk of confusing participants. If an AI assistant produces the challenge, label it Simulation on screen. Keep the response specific. “We have it handled” tells the room nothing. “We will review support tickets after the first cohort and stop if unresolved access questions rise” is a proposed plan that can be inspected. The precise threshold belongs in the learning plan before exposure. Rehearsal is valuable because it sharpens the next human conversation.

scenes.title: Write two sixty-second versions
scenes.narration: Draft the first sixty-second version for the operations owner. Name the decision, the delivery change, the review date, and what would stop the test. lessons.title: Governance and the system that learns

scenes.title: A local win creates a new problem
scenes.narration: One small test was useful. A second team asks to run it too. That sounds like progress, and it may be. It also changes the shape of the work. The first team knew the people, the context, and the reason for every field in its learning plan. The second team receives a template and a sentence about success. Context can disappear between those two moments. Chapter Twenty-Four asks what changes at scale: experiments can collide, metrics can mean different things, and a tool can spread faster than a review practice. Treat the original test from our fictional membership service as a candidate for reuse, not an approved model. What was the job? Which participants were in scope? What did the team observe? Which result is still pending? If the new team serves people with a different access need, the first team's conclusion may not travel. Put the source and exclusion beside the result. Scaling begins with a transfer of judgment. The useful question is whether another team can reproduce the decision boundary, not whether it can copy the screen. Start the scale-readiness checklist with the parts that must travel: definition, owner, evidence, stop condition, and a place to record the next result. At this point, speed can become a source of error. The first team may know that an apparent improvement came from a narrow group, or that a support burden rose after the measurement window. A copied summary loses both facts. Ask the original owner to mark what another team must verify again. Make that conversation part of the handoff, then record the answer so the next team does not rely on hallway memory.

scenes.title: Use a light common record
scenes.narration: The book proposes shared infrastructure: an experiment template, a hypothesis backlog, and a decision log. These are not three new committees. They are ways to keep a test understandable after the original team moves on. Write a one-page record. It names the customer job, hypothesis, eligibility rule, measure, decision threshold, date, and reviewer. Add links to the source ledger and any observed result. Give the next team permission to say its context differs. A common format makes differences easier to see. Chapter Twenty-Four also warns that a central learning team can become a bottleneck. Assign a local owner who can run the test within an agreed boundary, and a cross-team reviewer for conflicts or shared risk. The governance should fit the consequence. A copy change might need a quick review. A change to pricing, access, privacy, or billing needs the people who own those obligations. This is the practical meaning of light governance: enough common language to coordinate, enough local authority to keep learning, and a clear escalation path when the cost of being wrong rises. The record should help work move, not make people prove that they filled every box. Use the template as a doorway into judgment. A reviewer should be able to spot a missing source or conflicting test without reading a novel. Show who has authority to pause work when an access or privacy problem appears. Write the escalation in ordinary language. If nobody can tell who owns the next decision, the process is too vague to protect the people involved. If every minor edit waits for a central committee, it is too heavy to help them.

scenes.title: Find the five failure modes
scenes.narration: Chapter Twenty-Four names five scaling mistakes. A central team can become a bottleneck. Documentation can grow so heavy that people stop testing. The organization can fixate on one tool instead of shared learning. Teams can resist a process they did not help shape. And leaders can expand across the whole organization before the first handoff works. Put those five labels on the checklist and test your own proposal against them. Which one is most likely here? In the fictional membership case, tool fixation could be tempting: the first team has a spreadsheet, so everyone is told to use the same spreadsheet. What matters is whether the second team can understand the hypothesis, measure, and decision. Another tool could carry the same record if it preserves the contract. Resistance can also be information. Ask what work the new team already does and what burden the process would add. A five-minute decision note may fit; a fifty-page report will likely disappear into the backlog. The chapter's maturity question is powerful: can a new colleague explain why the organization passed on an obvious alternative, citing the decision record? If the answer lives only in one person's memory, the system has not yet traveled. Check the next-team burden before declaring the system ready. Have someone outside the first team fill out the record with a fictional case. Note which fields they cannot interpret and which handoffs require a conversation. Revise the form before a live rollout. Keep the five book labels attached to this check; they are a useful warning, not a score or maturity ranking. A low score invented for the slide would add confidence without evidence.

scenes.title: Keep Sam's story in its lane
scenes.narration: Chapter Twenty-Five returns to Sam. The book describes a calmer operating rhythm: fewer frantic searches for context, shorter decisions, and a record that people can find. This is the book's illustration. It is not evidence that our fictional membership service, AmaduTown, or this workshop has produced those outcomes. The story is useful because it shows what institutional memory feels like in daily work. Someone asks why a choice was made. Instead of rebuilding the argument from old messages, the team opens the decision log. Someone wants to repeat a test. Instead of copying a result without context, they can inspect the participants, measure, and revision. Notice how much of this depends on people. A record must be written well enough to be read; a reviewer must notice when evidence no longer fits; an owner must still decide. Automated routing can move a source to the right place. It cannot determine whether a past finding applies to a different community. In the storyboard, keep Sam's narrative label separate from any observed evidence card. We will not film a fabricated board meeting as if it happened in the present project. The before-and-after story can tempt us to promise relief too early. Ask what would have to be measured to make that claim in a real organization: time spent finding context, repeated decisions, missed handoffs, and the cost of maintaining the records. A calmer calendar alone would not explain why it changed. Keep the causal claim open until the evidence can support it. The lesson is a working rhythm that people can inspect, revise, and own.

scenes.title: Make the decision recoverable
scenes.narration: The decision-memory record is where a useful test becomes a reusable asset. Write what the team believed before the test. Link to the source evidence. Record what happened, including contrary observations and limits. State the choice, the person accountable for it, and the condition that would reopen it. Add the date when its context should be checked again. If the decision was to defer, say why. If the result contradicted the hypothesis, keep it visible. A later team should be able to ask a narrow question: does this past decision still apply to our people and our operating constraints? The book's Sam story treats searchable decisions as part of a learning system. We can borrow that practice without borrowing its claimed numbers. For the membership exercise, a record might say the short-commitment offer remains a hypothesis until an approved test is reviewed. It should not say the model works. Link the two-audience pitch from Lesson Fourteen, the learning plan from Lesson Eight, and the job card from Lesson Twelve. Now the record shows the chain from input to interpretation to test to choice. If a source is missing, mark it. Recoverability depends on honest gaps as much as on good summaries. Imagine the original owner leaves. Can the next person find the most recent source, the decision threshold, and the reason an alternative was rejected? If not, add that missing link. If an AI summary is attached, preserve the original record beside it and name the human who checked the summary. The memory is only as reliable as the path back to its evidence. A confident paragraph without source links will age badly.

scenes.title: Decide whether to spread
scenes.narration: Pause and complete two pages. First, the scale-readiness checklist: common definition, participant boundary, measure, owner, review cadence, conflict check, privacy or billing escalation, and stop rule. Mark each field ready, missing, or context-dependent. Second, the decision-memory record: original question, evidence, test, outcome state, decision, rejected alternative, rationale, and revisit date. Resume when a second team could explain what it may reuse and what it must validate again. If your current evidence is only a synthetic workshop exercise, mark the scale decision blocked. Do not turn a hypothetical success into a rollout plan. In your own organization, keep private records inside approved systems and use only public, synthetic, or approved data here. The book gives us Sam's operating story and a set of governance problems to watch. The exercise asks for a smaller, inspectable answer: can another team find the evidence and know who can stop the test? The final lesson returns to the decision you named at the start. We will choose one move for the next week and give it a real review date. Learning becomes infrastructure when another person can pick up the record and act with the same care. End with a decision about readiness, even if the answer is wait. Choose one neighboring team for a future handoff only after the record survives a dry run. State which safeguards belong to the shared process and which must be set locally. This keeps a successful local experiment from becoming an organization-wide promise by accident. The aim is a repeatable learning practice that can carry disagreement and correction as well as success.

scenes.title: Return to the first decision
scenes.narration: Go back to the decision you wrote on the first page. At the time, it may have been a broad request: improve onboarding, grow revenue, or use AI to move faster. The file now gives that request edges. It names the person served, the evidence that exists, the alternatives considered, the test that could change the choice, and the people who must review it. Chapter Twenty-Six calls for starting with one pain point. That is the right size for the next week. Look at the Signals, Alignment, and Momentum labels on the approved Accelerated SAM infographic. They describe the path we have practiced: notice a signal, align a choice, and keep the learning available for the next decision. The art is a map, not a claim that your organization has finished the journey. Which question in your file is both important and answerable in seven days? Choose one. If the evidence is too weak for a launch, the next move may be an interview, a source audit, or a prototype test. A smaller honest move is more valuable than a large promise that cannot be checked.

scenes.title: Show how the file changed
scenes.narration: Sam appears again in the final chapter. A junior colleague can find a past decision and use it without asking her to reconstruct the whole story. The evidence ledger and living persona show what you know about the job and what remains uncertain. The roadmap and PRD trace keep the test connected to implementation. The ten-component learning plan names the measure and tripwire. The influence map shows who needs which evidence. The strategy and concept cards show a possible future without treating it as fact. The governance pages tell a second team what can travel. If one page contradicts another, fix the record now. The goal is not a beautiful binder. It is a decision another person can understand, challenge, and revisit. Pick the one unresolved question that matters most to the next move.

scenes.title: Set a seven-day test
scenes.narration: Write the next action in a sentence that begins with a verb. Interview three approved participants about the first task. Review six source notes with the service owner. Test two versions of a concept with a small, eligible group. The examples are options, not prescriptions, and their numbers are exercise sizes, not customer outcomes. Choose the move that fits your actual permission and capacity. Add a person who owns it. Add a review date within the next seven days. Decide in advance what evidence you will collect and where it will be stored. Name one observation that would make you revise the idea and one condition that would stop the test. If the work touches sensitive data, pricing, access, or a promise to a customer, bring the authorized owner into the design before acting. A model can help organize the question or draft a card. It cannot grant consent, approve a change, or absorb responsibility for a result. The final chapter's call to start small becomes practical when the small step has a date and a person attached to it.

scenes.title: Protect the boundary
scenes.narration: Before you schedule the review, inspect the source labels. An observed note records what a person actually said or did under an approved process. An interpretation states what you think it means. A simulation suggests a question to ask. These three can sit in one decision file, but they cannot be merged into one claim. The same applies to the book's cases. StratQuest, VisionScope, MarketCraft, Persuasive GPT, and Sam's story belong to the book. They offered teaching frames; they do not establish that a tool is deployed here or that a result happened in your organization. If your next action depends on a result you have only imagined, move the action back to validation. If it depends on private records, keep those records in the system that is authorized to hold them. Use public, synthetic, or approved material for this workshop. Good boundaries make learning possible because the team can tell what it is allowed to use, what still needs consent, and what remains a hypothesis. That clarity makes the next decision easier to trust.

scenes.title: Plan the review conversation
scenes.narration: Put a short review on the calendar with the owner and anyone whose work or access the test affects. Send the decision question and the source links in advance. At the meeting, open with what happened, including the observations that complicate your preferred story. Compare the result with the threshold you wrote before the test. Record one of four next states: continue, revise, stop, or gather a specific missing piece of evidence. Leave the outcome field blank until the review. The book's closing image is a system that grows through repeated choices, not a final piece of software to install once. Your first loop may be a page and a calendar reminder. That is enough if the page is honest and the reminder brings people back to a real decision. If the test fails, keep the learning. If it succeeds in one context, state that context before sharing it. A result becomes reusable when its limits travel with it. Give the next owner a record they can read without guessing what you meant. The chapter's One Year From Now passage imagines a large body of feedback, experiments, and decisions. Treat those figures as a possible future in the book, never as a forecast or a result promised by this course.

scenes.title: Close with one accountable move
scenes.narration: Pause and assemble the file. Put the one-week commitment on top: the decision, next action, owner, evidence to collect, review date, and stop or revision condition. Check that every claim below it carries a source or an uncertainty label. Resume when you can say the action aloud to another person and they can tell what will happen next. You do not need to run every tool named in the book. You do need a way to notice a problem, test a response, preserve the result, and let someone make the next choice with that knowledge. The final chapter says the system is unfinished. That is a useful ending because real work changes. People change. Conditions change. A decision file should make revision possible without erasing the path that brought you here. Next week, do the one move you wrote down. Then return to the record. What did you observe? What did it change? Who needs to know? Write the answer, and the next loop begins.
